prompt.context: Back in the 1990s, Bain Capital bought Domino's Pizza, a nationwide chain. They wanted to identify a growth strategy. There are four national players: Pizza Hut is the market leader and owns mainly sit-down stores but also offers some delivery. Domino's has no sit-down restaurants and no carry-outs; its entire operation is built around delivery; 80% of stores are franchisees and 20% are company-owned. Little Caesar's marketing campaign is 2 pies for the price of 1; their restaurants are cafeteria-style with carry-out and no delivery. Papa John's is a new player with very fast growth; no sit-down restaurants; their entire model is carry-out because stores are located on high foot-traffic streets; their marketing strategy is 'better ingredients, better pizza.' In a blind taste test, despite little taste preference between the four pizzas, when brand names were revealed people chose Papa John's.
prompt.question: Bain Capital has acquired Domino's Pizza and wants to identify a growth strategy. What would you recommend?

clarifying_info.q: What are Luigi's (franchisee) costs per pizza?
What royalty does Domino's receive from franchisees?
What is the current price and volume for Luigi's store?
clarifying_info.a: Luigi currently sells 100 pizzas per day at $10 each; if he raises the price to $11, he will sell 90 per day.

framework: Industry landscape: map the four national players, their formats (delivery vs. carry-out vs. sit-down), and competitive positioning
Growth opportunities: identify levers to grow Domino's — new store openings, same-store sales growth, pricing
Site selection criteria for new stores: demographics, income, competition, costs, presence gaps
Unit economics: evaluate price changes at the store level (franchisee perspective)
Chain-level economics: evaluate price changes from Domino's corporate perspective (royalty on revenue)
Franchise price control: mechanisms to align franchisee incentives with corporate revenue goals
Recommendation: synthesize findings into a prioritized action plan

questions.prompt: What would you look at to identify where to open new stores?
questions.guidance: Strong answers cover multiple dimensions and go one level deeper on each: (1) Best practices — analyze existing high-performing stores to understand what locations work; (2) Competitive density — find regions with low competitor concentration including other fast food; (3) Cost structure — target markets with affordable labor and rent; (4) Demographics — pizza skews young (ages 13-35); (5) Income level — low-to-middle income preferred (high-income consumers favor sit-down restaurants); (6) Population growth — market should be growing, not declining; (7) Domino's presence gaps — white-space markets where Domino's is absent but demand exists; (8) Pizza demand trends — markets where overall pizza demand is growing. Wrap up by noting that ideally all factors align before opening a store.

questions.prompt: What specific type of location would be a good candidate for a new Domino's store?
questions.guidance: University neighborhoods are a strong answer: fits the young demographic, students tend to order delivery to dorms (plays to Domino's core strength), university enrollment typically grows year over year. Other strong answers: suburban strip malls, vicinity of office parks, near suburban schools, near sporting facilities. Interviewee should explain the reasoning behind each suggestion.

questions.prompt: Luigi currently sells 100 pizzas/day at $10 each. If he raises the price to $11, he will sell 90/day. His variable cost is $6/pizza. Should Luigi raise his price?
questions.guidance: Candidate should proactively ask for cost data before calculating. Bonus points for noting that fixed costs are irrelevant in the short run (same in both scenarios). Compare contribution profit at each price point.

math.setup: Compare daily profit at $10 vs. $11, with variable cost of $6/pizza.
math.answer: Yes, Luigi should raise his price. He earns $50 more per day.

questions.prompt: Would raising the price benefit Domino's corporate as a whole?
questions.guidance: Candidate must recall that Domino's is primarily a franchise business and ask about the royalty structure. Domino's earns 5% of franchisee revenues (not profits). Therefore, the revenue base (price x quantity) — not the franchisee's margin — drives Domino's take. A price increase that reduces total revenue hurts Domino's corporate even if it helps Luigi.

math.setup: Domino's earns 5% of franchisee sales revenue. Compare daily royalty at $10 vs. $11.
math.answer: No. Domino's corporate revenue falls by $0.50/day. The chain should not raise prices; Domino's should strictly control franchisee pricing.

questions.prompt: What can Domino's do to control prices among its stores — first with Luigi, then nationally?
questions.guidance: For Luigi: Explain to him that the price increase is only a short-term gain; in the long run, demand is elastic and customers will defect to competing pizza chains. Reinforce this with blind taste-test data showing that consumers view all pizzas as comparable (except Papa John's due to brand perception), meaning Domino's customers are price-sensitive and easy to lose. Nationally: Amend franchise contracts to include a pricing clause prohibiting price changes without corporate approval. For stores still under existing contracts: use national advertising to publicize a 'suggested price of $10' so consumers know when they are being overcharged, creating customer-pressure on franchisees to hold the line.

brainstorming.prompt: What factors would you analyze to identify the best locations to open new Domino's stores?

categories.name: Demand & Demographics
ideas: Low-to-middle income neighborhoods (high-income skews toward sit-down dining)
Population growing or at least stable
Pizza demand trend growing in the market

categories.name: Competitive Landscape
ideas: Regions with low concentration of pizza competitors
Regions with low concentration of other fast food (e.g., McDonald's)
Markets where Domino's currently has no presence

categories.name: Operational Fit
ideas: Domino's delivery model — areas where residents prefer delivery over carry-out
Dense residential or office areas reachable by delivery drivers

categories.name: Cost Structure
ideas: Proximity to supply chain for ingredient costs

categories.name: Internal Best Practices
ideas: Study existing high-performing stores to identify common location attributes
Replicate the profile of profitable stores in new markets

recommendation: Open new stores in high-potential locations: university neighborhoods, suburban strip malls, and office-park vicinities that match the target demographic (ages 13-35, low-to-middle income) and favor delivery over carry-out
Do not raise prices: a price increase reduces Domino's corporate royalty revenue because the company earns 5% of franchisee sales, and higher prices reduce total revenue

Control franchisee pricing: add explicit pricing clauses to new franchise contracts and use national advertising to publish suggested retail prices to discourage unauthorized price hikes by existing franchisees
risks: Franchisees in year 1 of 5-year contracts cannot immediately be compelled by contract; advertising pressure is the main lever in the short term
Demand elasticity may be higher than Luigi assumes — if customers defect quickly, his $50/day gain will be short-lived
New store openings require capital and site-selection rigor; poor site choices dilute brand and reduce franchisee viability
next_steps: Conduct a data-driven site-selection analysis using the criteria above (demographics, competition, cost, presence gaps)
Renegotiate or amend franchise contracts to include pricing-control provisions
Launch national advertising with explicit pricing to deter franchisee price increases
Pilot 2-3 new store formats (e.g., university-adjacent) to validate the site-selection thesis before broad rollout
